title: Cadences
intro: A cadence is the harmonic punctuation at the end of a phrase. Some close fully, like a full stop; some pause on the dominant, like a comma; some sidestep the expected ending.

items: Authentic cadence: V(7)–I. A perfect authentic cadence (PAC) has both chords in root position and the tonic in the top voice at the end; it is the strongest ending. An imperfect authentic cadence (IAC) has 3̂ or 5̂ on top, or an inverted chord.

Half cadence (HC): ends on V, approached by any chord (often IV, ii6 or I6/4). It sounds open, a question waiting for an answer. The Phrygian half cadence, iv6–V in minor, has the bass falling a semitone (6̂–5̂).
Plagal cadence: IV–I, the 'Amen' at the end of hymns. Usually an extension after an authentic cadence rather than the main close.
Deceptive cadence: V–vi (V–VI in minor). The ear expects I and gets its substitute, so the phrase must continue to a real cadence.

examples.label: Phrygian half cadence in A minor (iv6–V)

blocks.text: A cadence closes a phrase, the basic unit of musical thought (often four or eight bars). Pairs of phrases are commonly linked as an antecedent ending with a half cadence and a consequent ending with an authentic cadence: question and answer. The Form (#/arts/music-theory/form) chapter builds on this.

Play a PAC in all twelve keys: left hand 5̂ to 1̂ in octaves, right hand moving 7̂ up to 1̂ and 4̂ down to 3̂ (the tritone resolving). Then turn it into a deceptive cadence by moving the left hand up a step to 6̂ instead of down to 1̂; the right hand barely changes.

items: Step 1. Perfect authentic cadence in C: left hand G3 then C3; right hand D4–F4–B4 resolving to C4–E4–C5 (B up to C, F down to E, D down to C). Hear the full stop.
Step 2. Half cadence: end the same phrase on G (V) instead: it sounds like a question.
Step 3. Deceptive cadence: play G7 and then, instead of C, move the bass up a step to A3 with the right hand on C4–E4–C5: A minor. It sounds like a surprise.
Step 4. Plagal cadence: F to C (IV–I), the 'Amen' at the end of hymns.
Step 5. Step through each cadence on the keyboard above, copying the chords.

blocks.title: Name the cadence
blocks.text: A phrase in G major ends C–D. Another ends D7–Em. Name each cadence.
solution: C–D is IV–V: a half cadence. D7–Em is V7–vi: a deceptive cadence.

blocks.title: PAC or IAC
blocks.text: A phrase ends V–I with both chords in root position and the melody ending on 3̂. Is it perfect or imperfect?
solution: A PAC needs root-position V and I and 1̂ in the top voice. With 3̂ on top it is imperfect (IAC).

blocks.text: Sources: Caplin, W. E. (1998). Classical Form. Oxford University Press; Aldwell, E., Schachter, C. & Cadwallader, A. (2019). Harmony and Voice Leading, 5th ed. Cengage; Kostka, S., Payne, D. & Almén, B. (2018). Tonal Harmony, 8th ed. McGraw-Hill.
